title: Daniel Kahneman, a psychologist born in Tel Aviv, showed how people make decisions and won the Nobel Prize in Economics

trailer.text: He was born in 1934 in Tel Aviv and held Israeli and American citizenship.
According to the Swedish Academy's announcement, Kahneman showed that human decisions may systematically depart from what economic theory predicts.
Together with Amos Tversky, he formulated prospect theory, an alternative that better accounts for the behavior actually observed.
According to JTA, this work helped change economists' approach and effectively launched the field of behavioral economics.

stations.title: A Jewish boy in occupied Paris

paragraphs.text: Kahneman was born in Tel Aviv while his mother was visiting her extended family there, but the family's permanent home was in Paris.
According to JTA, his parents were Jews of Lithuanian origin, and he grew up in France, where his father worked as a representative of a cosmetics company.
During the Nazi occupation, the family was forced to move again and again.
In an interview with The Guardian, he said he felt hunted, like rabbits.
Kahneman also told of an SS soldier who picked him up and hugged him, while he was afraid the soldier would see the Star of David under his sweater.
He wrote that after the encounter he went home more certain than ever that his mother was right: people are endlessly complicated and interesting.
His father died six weeks before D-Day.
Afterwards, Kahneman, his mother and his sister moved to Palestine.
According to JTA, Kahneman served in the Israeli army from 1954.

According to the same source, when he was a professor of psychology at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, he gave the Israeli military important insights into how to motivate soldiers and reduce mistakes in the heat of battle.
In the IDF Psychology Branch, he noticed the gap between assessments of officer candidates on an obstacle course and what they actually did.
Kahneman then wrote a doctoral dissertation, which was submitted in 1961.
According to Social Science Space, Amitai Etzioni, at Berkeley
Their long collaboration began after Tversky gave a guest lecture in Kahneman's seminar.
In 1974 the article Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases was published in Science, and it was widely read.
According to NPR, Kahneman wrote that some decisions are influenced by shortcuts that fall into predictable patterns.
A gambler or an investor, for example, might take more risks after a loss.
According to NPR, their research identified irrational decisions that can be understood.
One example: judges grant more paroles after lunch than when they are hungry.
The peak-end rule holds that our impression of a past event is determined mainly by its peak moment and its final moment, and not by the total amount of pleasure and suffering.

According to one of the sources, in the mid-1970s, when Kahneman was at Stanford as a fellow at the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences, he also began working with the economist Richard Thaler on what was termed the endowment effect and mental accounting.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded Kahneman the 2002 Prize in Economics.
He received it for integrating insights from psychological research into economic science, especially concerning judgment and decision-making under uncertainty.
According to the announcement, economics was generally considered a science that looks at real economies rather than conducting controlled laboratory experiments.
Kahneman shared the prize with Vernon Smith, who won for establishing laboratory experiments as a tool for economic analysis.
The prize amount, 10 million Swedish kronor, was shared equally between the two laureates.
At the time, Kahneman was a professor of psychology and public affairs at Princeton University, a position he had held since 1993.
He also said he had never taken even a single course in economics.
According to the Hon website, this is what sets him apart among Nobel laureates in economics: his field of expertise is psychology.

stations.title: A new field and a book for everyone

paragraphs.text: According to the Academy's announcement, Kahneman's work inspired a new generation of researchers in economics and finance, who enriched economic theory with insights from cognitive psychology.
According to the Hon website, his insights created and established behavioral economics.
Social Science Space called him "The Grandfather of Behavioral Economics".
In 2011 his book Thinking, Fast and Slow was published, and according to JTA it sold more than a million copies around the world.
In the book he described two kinds of thinking: fast thinking, intuitive and emotional, and slow thinking, more deliberate and logical.
In 2021 he published, with Olivier Sibony and Cass Sunstein, the best-seller Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment.
At Princeton, Kahneman, together with Eldar Shafir, developed the first psychology for policy course at the School of Public and International Affairs.
In 2015, a $10 million gift from an anonymous donor funded the establishment of the Kahneman-Treisman Center at the university.
Kahneman and Tversky jointly received the Grawemeyer Award.
In 2013, President Barack Obama awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
Princeton's president, Christopher Eisgruber, said that Kahneman changed our understanding of rationality and its limits.
According to NPR, Kahneman himself credited much of his success to good luck.
According to Social Science Space, in 2002
According to JTA, Kahneman told The Guardian that he was on the far left of the Israeli political spectrum.
According to the same source, he was pessimistic about the prospects for peace between Israelis and Palestinians.
According to Princeton University, Kahneman died on March 27, 2024, at the age of 90.
Social Science Space described Thinking, Fast and Slow as readable and erudite pop science, but perhaps a bit too facile.
Nathan Novemsky, whose doctoral advisor was Kahneman, said that the field Kahneman helped found learned decades later that a little more scientific self-doubt would be helpful for all of us.
